nodes.name: Gaussian binomial coefficients
nodes.statement: The Gaussian binomial coefficients are defined by \begin{equation} \dbinom{n}{r}_q = \begin{cases} \frac{(1-q^n)(1-q^{n-1})\cdots(1-q^{n-r+1})}{(1-q)(1-q^2)\cdots(1-q^r)} & \text{if $r\le n$}\\ 0 & \text{if $r > n$}, \end{cases} \end{equation} where with $\mid q \mid < 1$ .
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus et al.; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas et al.; Podlubny; Samko et al.; Kac & Cheung (sources of Section 2.1)
nodes.statement_short: Defines the $q$-binomial coefficient as a ratio of products of $(1-q^k)$, zero when $r>n$.

nodes.name: Gaussian binomial coefficient formula
nodes.statement: \dbinom{n}{r}_q = \begin{cases} \frac{(1-q^n)(1-q^{n-1})\cdots(1-q^{n-r+1})}{(1-q)(1-q^2)\cdots(1-q^r)} & \text{if $r\le n$}\\ 0 & \text{if $r > n$}, \end{cases}
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus et al.; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas et al.; Podlubny; Samko et al.; Kac & Cheung (sources of Section 2.1)

nodes.name: q-Pascal identity for Gaussian binomial coefficients
nodes.statement: \dbinom{n}{r}_q = q^r \dbinom{n-1}{r}_q + \dbinom{n-1}{r-1}_q.

nodes.name: Beta function
nodes.statement: The beta function is defined as: \begin{equation} B(p,q) = \int_{0}^1 x^{p-1} (1-x)^{1-q}dx, \quad \textrm{for}\quad Re(p), Re(q)>0. \end{equation} We have \begin{equation} B(p,q) =\frac{\Gamma (p) \Gamma (q)}{\Gamma{(p+q)}}. \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus et al.; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas et al.; Podlubny; Samko et al.; Kac & Cheung (sources of Section 2.1)

nodes.name: Regularized incomplete beta function

nodes.name: Kummer's confluent hypergeometric functions
nodes.statement: Kummer's confluent hyper-geometric functions $_{1}F_{1}(a;c;x)$ and $U(a;c;x)$ are defined as below \begin{equation} _{1}F_{1}(a;c;x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(a)_n}{(c)_n} \frac{x^n}{n!},\quad c\ne 0,-1,-2,\cdots \textrm{and} \end{equation} \begin{equation} U(a;c;x) = \frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi c)}\left(\frac{_{1}F_{1}(a;c;x)}{\Gamma(c)\Gamma(1+a-c)}-x^{1-c}\frac{_{1}F_{1}(1+a-c;2-c;x)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(2-c)}\right), \end{equation} \begin{equation} -\pi<arg (x) \leq \pi.\nonumber \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus et al.; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas et al.; Podlubny; Samko et al.; Kac & Cheung (sources of Section 2.1)
nodes.statement_short: Defines Kummer's $_1F_1$ as a Pochhammer power series and Tricomi's $U$ as a combination of two $_1F_1$'s.

nodes.name: Space $C_\alpha$
nodes.statement: A real function $f(x)$, $x>0$, is said to be in space $C_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, if there exists a real number $p (>\alpha)$, such that $f(x)=x^p f_1(x) $ where $f_1(x)\in C[0,\infty)$.

nodes.name: Riemann-Liouville integral
nodes.statement: Let $f\in C_\alpha $ and $\alpha \geq -1$, then the (left-sided) Riemann-Liouville integral of order $\mu, \mu> 0 $ is given by \begin{equation} I^\mu f(t)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\mu)} \int_{0}^t (t-\tau)^{\mu-1}f(\tau)d\tau,\quad t>0. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Caputo fractional derivative
nodes.statement: The (left sided) Caputo fractional derivative of $f, f \in C_{-1}^m, m\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$, is defined as: \begin{eqnarray} D^\mu f(t)&=&\frac{d^m}{ dt^m} f(t),\quad \mu = m \nonumber\\ &=& I^{m-\mu}\frac{d^m}{ dt^m} f(t),\quad {m-1} <\mu <m,\quad m\in \mathbb{N}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.origin_citation: Magnus et al.; Luchko & Gorenflo; Kilbas et al.; Podlubny; Samko et al.; Kac & Cheung (sources of Section 2.1)

nodes.statement_short: Fractional integral of $(x-b)^\beta$, and $I^\alpha D^\alpha f$ equals $f$ minus its Taylor polynomial at 0.

nodes.name: Daftardar-Gejji and Jafari Method (DJM)
nodes.statement: Suppose that given problem can be transformed to the model equation \begin{equation} u= f + L(u) + N(u), \end{equation} where $L$ and $N$ are linear and nonlinear operators respectively and $f$ is known function.\\ In this case, the DJM provides the solution in the form of series \begin{equation} u= \sum_{i=0}^\infty u_i. \end{equation} where $u_0=f,\; u_1=N(u_0)\;$ and \begin{equation} u_{n+1} = N\left(\sum_{j=0}^n u_j\right)- N\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} u_j\right), \quad n=1, 2, \cdots. \\ \end{equation} Usually, the k-term approximate solution $u= \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} u_i$ is used to approximate the exact solution.
nodes.statement_short: Iterative series method for $u=f+L(u)+N(u)$: $u_0=f$, $u_{n+1}$ from differences of $N$ on partial sums; truncate after $k$ terms.

nodes.statement_short: Set $u_0=f$, $u_1=N(u_0)$ and compute $u_{n+1}$ recursively.

nodes.statement: \cite{CONV} If $N$ is $C^{(\infty)}$ in a neighborhood of $y_0$ and $\left\|N^{(n)}(y_0) \right\| \leq L$, for any $n$ and for some real $L>0$ and $\left\|y_i\right\| \leq M <\frac{1}{e}$, $i=1,2,\cdots,$ then the series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} G_n$ is absolutely convergent to $N$ and moreover, \begin{equation*} \left\|G_n\right\| \leq L M^n e^{n-1} (e-1), \quad n=1,2,\cdots. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: If $N$ is smooth with bounded derivatives and the iterates are small, the DJM series converges absolutely with geometric term bounds.

nodes.name: Convergence of DJM series

nodes.name: Proportional-delay equation as a time-dependent delay DDE
nodes.statement: The equation \begin{equation} y'(t) = f\left(t, y(t), y(pt)\right), \end{equation} is a particular case of time dependent delay differential equation (DDE) \begin{equation} y'(t) = f\left(t, y(t), y\left(t-\tau(t)\right)\right)\quad \textrm{with}\quad\tau(t)=(1-p)t. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $y'=f(t,y(t),y(pt))$ is a time-dependent-delay DDE with $\tau(t)=(1-p)t$.

nodes.name: Local existence theorem
nodes.statement: (\textbf{Local existence})\\ Consider the equation \begin{eqnarray} y'(t)&=& f\left(t, y(t), y\left(t-\tau(t)\right)\right),\quad t_0 \leq t < t_f,\nonumber\\ y(t_0)&=& y_0, \end{eqnarray} and assume that the function $f(t,u,v)$ is continuous on $A \subseteq [t_0,t_f)\times\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^m$ and locally Lipschitz continuous with respect to u and v. Moreover, assume that the delay function $\tau(t)\geq 0$ is continuous in $[t_0,t_f)$, $\tau(t_0)=0$ and, for some $\xi > 0 $, $t-\tau(t) > t_0$ in the interval $(t_0, t_0+\xi]$. Then the problem (\ref{pro1}) has a unique solution in $[t_0,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta >0$ and this solution depends continuously on the initial data.
nodes.statement_short: Continuous, locally Lipschitz $f$ and a vanishing-at-$t_0$ delay give a unique local solution depending continuously on data.

nodes.name: Global existence theorem
nodes.statement: (\textbf{Global existence})\\ Under the hypothesis of Theorem \ref{th1}, if the unique maximal solution of (\ref{pro1}) is bounded, then it exist on the entire interval $[t_0,t_f)$.
assumptions: the unique maximal solution of (\ref{pro1}) is bounded

nodes.name: First derivative of $\mathcal{R}$ at scaled argument
nodes.statement: For $0<q<1$, $a \in \mathbb{R}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{N} \cup\{0\} $, we have \begin{equation} \frac{d}{dx}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x)= a q^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x) + b q^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^{m+1}x). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement: Consider \begin{eqnarray*} \frac{d}{dx}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x) &=& \frac{d}{dx} \left( 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(q^m x)^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a + bq^j\right)\right)\\ &=& q^m\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(q^m x)^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a + bq^j\right)\\ &=& q^m (a+b) + q^m\sum_{n=2}^\infty\frac{(q^m x)^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a + bq^j\right)\\ &=& q^m (a+b) + q^m\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(q^m x)^{n}}{{n}!}\prod_{j=0}^{n}\left(a + bq^j\right)\\ &=& q^m (a+b) + q^m\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(q^m x)^{n}(a+bq^n)}{{n}!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a + bq^j\right)\\ &=& aq^m \left( 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(q^m x)^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a + bq^j\right)\right)\\ && + bq^m \left( 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(q^{m+1}x)^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a + bq^j\right)\right)\\ \frac{d}{dx}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x) &=& a q^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x) + b q^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^{m+1}x) \end{eqnarray*} Hence the proof.

nodes.statement: \frac{d^m}{dx^m}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) &=& \frac{d}{dx} \left(\frac{d^{m-1}}{dx^{m-1}}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)\right)\\ &=& \frac{d}{dx} \left( \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-(r+1)} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^r x)\right)\\ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-(r+1)} b^r \frac{d}{dx}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^r x).

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 4.2 and reindex
nodes.statement:
Using Theorem [ef{6.1.3}], we have  egin{eqnarray*}  rac{d^m}{dx^m}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-(r+1)} b^r 
onumber\ &&\left( a q^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx) + b q^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^{r+1}x)ight)\ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)\ &&+ \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{k}{2}} q^k \dbinom{m-1}{k}_q a^{m-(k+1)} b^{k+1} \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^{k+1}x) \end{eqnarray*}  egin{eqnarray*} &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)\ && + \sum_{k=1}^{m} q^{\dbinom{k}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{k-1}_q a^{m-k} b^k \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^kx)\ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)
onumber\ && - q^{\dbinom{m}{2}} q^m \dbinom{m-1}{m}_q b^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^m x) \ && + \sum_{k=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{k}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{k-1}_q a^{m-k} b^k \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^kx) 
onumber\ && - \dbinom{m-1}{-1}_q a^m \mathcal{R}(a,b,q, x) \ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx)\ && + \sum_{k=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{k}{2}} \dbinom{m-1}{k-1}_q a^{m-k} b^k q^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^kx) \ &=& \sum_{r=0}^{m} q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \left(q^r \dbinom{m-1}{r}_q + \dbinom{m-1}{r-1}_q ight) a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx). \end{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: Apply q-Pascal identity
nodes.statement: Using identity (\ref{6.1.2}), \begin{equation} \frac{d^m}{dx^m}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)= \sum_{r=0}^m q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{m}{r}_q a^{m-r} b^r \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,q^rx), \end{equation} This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Combine with the $q$-Pascal identity to obtain the formula for $m$.

nodes.name: Gaussian binomial expansion of $\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: For $0<q<1$, we have \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r \frac{x^n}{n!}, \end{equation} where $\dbinom{n}{r}_q$ is the Gaussian binomial coefficient.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{R}$ expands as a double sum of Gaussian binomial coefficients times $a^{n-r}b^r x^n/n!$.

nodes.name: Gaussian binomial expansion formula
nodes.statement: \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r \frac{x^n}{n!},

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.4
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right). \end{equation} Using the $q$- binomial theorem \begin{equation} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right) = \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r, \end{equation} defined in \cite{Richard}, we obtain \begin{eqnarray} \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r\nonumber\\ \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r \frac{x^n}{n!}. \end{eqnarray} Hence the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the $q$-binomial theorem for the product in the defining series.

nodes.name: Recall series
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Recall the defining series of $\mathcal{R}$.

nodes.name: Apply q-binomial theorem
nodes.statement: Using the $q$- binomial theorem \begin{equation} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right) = \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r, \end{equation} defined in \cite{Richard}, we obtain \begin{eqnarray} \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r\nonumber\\ \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r \frac{x^n}{n!}. \end{eqnarray} Hence the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the $q$-binomial theorem to the product.

nodes.name: q-binomial theorem
nodes.statement: \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right) = \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r,

nodes.statement: \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r\nonumber\\ \mathcal{R}(a, b, q, x) &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}}\dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r}b^r \frac{x^n}{n!}.

nodes.name: Exponential bounds for $\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: For $0<q<1$, $a\ge 0$ and $b\ge 0$, the function $\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)$ satisfies the following inequality \begin{equation} e^{ax}\le \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)\le e^{(a+b)x},\quad 0 \le x < \infty. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Exponential bounds inequality
nodes.statement: e^{ax}\le \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)\le e^{(a+b)x},\quad 0 \le x < \infty.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.5
nodes.statement_short: Bound each product $\prod(a+bq^j)$ between $a^n$ and $(a+b)^n$ and sum the series.

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement_short: Termwise bound by $(a+b)^n$ gives $\mathcal{R}\le e^{(a+b)x}$.

nodes.name: Upper bound derivation
nodes.statement:
\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^jight) &\le& (a+b)^n 
onumber\ \Rightarrow  rac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^jight) &\le&  rac{x^n (a+b)^n}{n!}.
onumber\ 	extrm{Taking summation over n, we get} 
onumber\ \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) &\le& e^{(a+b)x},\quad 0 \le x < \infty.

nodes.name: Lower bound
nodes.statement: Similarly, we have \begin{eqnarray} a^n &\le& \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right) \nonumber\\ \Rightarrow e^{ax} &\le& \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) ,\quad 0 \le x < \infty. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Termwise bound by $a^n$ gives $e^{ax}\le\mathcal{R}$.

nodes.name: Lower bound derivation
nodes.statement: a^n &\le& \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right) \nonumber\\ \Rightarrow e^{ax} &\le& \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) ,\quad 0 \le x < \infty.

nodes.name: Combine bounds
nodes.statement: From (\ref{6.5.1}) and (\ref{6.5.2}), we get \begin{equation} e^{ax}\le \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)\le e^{(a+b)x},\quad 0 \le x < \infty. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Upper-incomplete integral of $e^{-t}\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt = \Gamma (1, x)\left(1+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \frac{x^k}{k!}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\int_x^\infty e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(t)dt$ equals $\Gamma(1,x)$ times a Gaussian-binomial series in $x$.

nodes.name: Integral of $e^{-t}\mathcal{R}$ over $[x,\infty)$
nodes.statement: \int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt = \Gamma (1, x)\left(1+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \frac{x^k}{k!}\right).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.6
nodes.statement: Consider \begin{eqnarray*} \int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& \int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t}t^n dt\\ &=& e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \Gamma(n+1,x)\\ &=& e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} n! e^{-x}\sum_{k=0}^n \frac{x^k}{k!}\\ &=& e^{-x}\left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{x^k}{k!}\right)\\ \int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)dt &=& \Gamma (1, x)\left(1+\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \frac{x^k}{k!}\right). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate termwise, express $\int_x^\infty e^{-t}t^n dt$ via $\Gamma(n+1,x)$, then its finite-sum form.

nodes.name: Lower-incomplete integral of $e^{-t}\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& 1+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \nonumber\\ && -\Gamma (1, x)\left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \frac{x^k}{k!}\right). \end{eqnarray}
conclusions: \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& 1+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \nonumber\\ && -\Gamma (1, x)\left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \frac{x^k}{k!}\right).

nodes.name: Integral of $e^{-t}\mathcal{R}$ over $[0,x]$
nodes.statement: \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& 1+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \nonumber\\ && -\Gamma (1, x)\left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \frac{x^k}{k!}\right).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.7
nodes.statement: Consider \begin{eqnarray*} \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& \int_{0}^xe^{-t} dt + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \int_{0}^xe^{-t}t^n dt\\ &=& 1- e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} \gamma(n+1,x)\\ &=& 1- e^{-x} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac {\left(a+bq^j\right)}{n!} n!\left( 1-e^{-x}\sum_{k=0}^n \frac{x^k}{k!}\right)\\ &=& 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \nonumber\\ && - e^{-x}\left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r\frac{x^k}{k!}\right)\;(\textrm{From (\ref{6.5.5})})\\ \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=& 1+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \nonumber\\ && -\Gamma (1, x)\left(1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{r=0}^n q^{\dbinom{r}{2}} \dbinom{n}{r}_q a^{n-r} b^r \frac{x^k}{k!}\right). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate termwise, use $\gamma(n+1,x)$ in finite-sum form and the $q$-binomial theorem.

nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray*} \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt &=&1 + \Gamma (1, x)\left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {x^n}{n!} {}_1F_{1}(1; n+1; x) - \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)\right)\\ &=& 1 -\Gamma (1, x) \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)\frac {x^n}{n!} {}_1F_{1}(n; n+1; -x). \end{eqnarray*}

onumber \end{eqnarray} Again using the relation (ef{6.1.15}) in 	extbf{ef{6.1.4}}, we get  egin{equation} \int_{0}^xe^{-t}\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,t)dt= 1 -\Gamma (1, x) \mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^jight) rac {x^n}{n!} {}_1F_{1}(n; n+1; -x)

nodes.name: Scaling property of $\mathcal{R}$ with $a=0$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}\left(0,\pm b^m,q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(0,1,q,\pm b^mx\right)$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{R}\left(0,\pm a^{l}b^{-m},q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(0,1,q,\pm a^{l}b^{-m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(0,\pm b^{-m},q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(0,1,q,\pm b^{-m}x\right)$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: $\mathcal{R}\left(0,\pm b^m,q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(0,1,q,\pm b^mx\right)$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{R}\left(0,\pm a^{l}b^{-m},q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(0,1,q,\pm a^{l}b^{-m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(0,\pm b^{-m},q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(0,1,q,\pm b^{-m}x\right)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: With $a=0$, a power of $b$ can be moved from the second parameter into the argument.

nodes.name: Scaling property of $\mathcal{R}$ with related $a$, $b$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}\left(a^m, a^m,q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,1,q,a^mx\right)$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{R}\left(\pm a^{-m}, \pm a^m,q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,a^{2m},q,\pm a^{-m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(\pm a^m, \pm a^{-m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,a^{-2m},q,\pm a^mx\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(-a^m, a^{-m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{-2m},q,-a^{m}x\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(a^m, -a^{-m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{-2m},q,a^{m}x\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(-a^{-m}, a^{m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{2m},q,-a^{-m}x\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(a^{-m}, -a^{m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{2m},q,a^{-m}x\right)$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: $\mathcal{R}\left(a^m, a^m,q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,1,q,a^mx\right)$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{R}\left(\pm a^{-m}, \pm a^m,q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,a^{2m},q,\pm a^{-m}x\right)$. \item $\mathcal{R}\left(\pm a^m, \pm a^{-m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,a^{-2m},q,\pm a^mx\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(-a^m, a^{-m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{-2m},q,-a^{m}x\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(a^m, -a^{-m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{-2m},q,a^{m}x\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(-a^{-m}, a^{m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{2m},q,-a^{-m}x\right)$. \item $ \mathcal{R}\left(a^{-m}, -a^{m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}\left(1,-a^{2m},q,a^{-m}x\right)$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Convergence of $\mathcal{R}_\alpha$
nodes.statement: If $0<q<1$, then the power series \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}_\alpha(a, b, q, x) =1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^{\alpha n}}{\Gamma{(\alpha n + 1)}}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^{\alpha j}\right), \end{equation} is convergent for all finite values of $x$.
conclusions: is convergent for all finite values of $x$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.1
nodes.statement: Result follows immediately by ratio test \begin{eqnarray*} \lim_{n\to\infty}\left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| &=& a \left|x\right|^\alpha \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac {\Gamma(\alpha n)}{\Gamma{(\alpha (n + 1))}}\\ &=& 0. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Ratio test: the ratio involves $\Gamma(\alpha n)/\Gamma(\alpha(n+1))\to 0$.

nodes.name: Scaling property of $\mathcal{R}_\alpha$ with $a=0$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(0,\pm b^{\alpha m},q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(0,1,q,\pm b^{\alpha m}x\right)$.

nodes.name: Scaling property of $\mathcal{R}_\alpha$ with equal parameters
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(a^{\alpha m}, a^{\alpha m},q,x\right) = \mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(1,1,q,a^{\alpha m}x\right)$.

nodes.name: Normalization of first parameter of $\mathcal{R}_\alpha$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(a^{\alpha l}, b^{\alpha m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(1, a^{-{\alpha m}} b^{\alpha m},q,a^{\alpha l}x\right)$ and so on.
conclusions: $\mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(a^{\alpha l}, b^{\alpha m}, q, x\right) = \mathcal{R}_\alpha\left(1, a^{-{\alpha m}} b^{\alpha m},q,a^{\alpha l}x\right)$ and so on.

nodes.statement: Consider the system of delay differential equation with proportional delay \begin{equation} Y'(x) = AY(x)+ BY(q x),\quad Y(0)= Y_0, \end{equation} where $0<q<1$, $A=\left(a_{ij}\right)_{n\times n}$, $B=\left(b_{ij}\right)_{n\times n}$ and $Y=$ $ \begin{bmatrix} y_1\\ y_2\\ \vdots\\ y_n \end{bmatrix}. $
nodes.statement_short: Matrix IVP $Y'=AY(x)+BY(qx)$, $Y(0)=Y_0$, $0<q<1$.

nodes.name: Matrix Ramanujan function $\overline{\mathcal{R}}(A,B,q,xI)$
nodes.statement: We denote this series by \begin{equation} \overline{\mathcal{R}}(A, B, q, xI) = \left( I + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(A+Bq^{n-j}\right)\right)Y_0. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Series of $\overline{\mathcal{R}}$
nodes.statement: \overline{\mathcal{R}}(A, B, q, xI) = \left( I + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(A+Bq^{n-j}\right)\right)Y_0.

nodes.name: Convergence of $\overline{\mathcal{R}}$
nodes.statement: If $0<q<1$, and $(A+Bq^n)$ is invertible for each $n$, then the power series \begin{equation} \overline{\mathcal{R}}(A, B, q, xI) = \left( I + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(A+Bq^{n-j}\right)\right)Y_0, \end{equation} where $A\in M_{n\times n}$ and $B\in M_{n\times n}$ is convergent for $x\in\mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.2
nodes.statement: By ratio test \cite{Lucas}, \begin{eqnarray*} &&\left\|\left(\frac{x^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\prod_{j=1}^{n+1}\left(A+Bq^{n+1-j}\right)\right)\left(\frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(A+Bq^{n-j}\right)\right)^{-1}\right\|\\ &=&\frac{\mid x \mid}{n+1} \left\|\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n+1}\left(A+Bq^{n+1-j}\right)\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(A+Bq^{n-j}\right)\right)^{-1}\right\| \\ &=&\frac{\mid x \mid}{n+1} \left\| A + Bq^n\right\|\\ &=& 0,\quad \textrm{as}\;n \longrightarrow \infty. \end{eqnarray*} $\therefore$ The power series (\ref{7.2.4}) is convergent for $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Matrix ratio test: the ratio norm is $|x|\,\|A+Bq^n\|/(n+1)\to 0$.

nodes.name: Scaling property of $\overline{\mathcal{R}}$ with $A=0$
nodes.statement: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(0,\pm B^m,q,xI\right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(0,I,q,\pm B^mx\right)$.

nodes.name: Scaling property of $\overline{\mathcal{R}}$ with equal parameters
nodes.statement: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A^m, A^m,q,xI\right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(I,I,q,A^mx\right)$, etc.

nodes.name: Contiguous relation of $\overline{\mathcal{R}}$ in $A$
nodes.statement: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A\pm I, B, q, xI\right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(I, (A \pm I)^{-1} B, q, (A \pm I)x\right)$.
conclusions: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A\pm I, B, q, xI\right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(I, (A \pm I)^{-1} B, q, (A \pm I)x\right)$.

nodes.name: Contiguous relation of $\overline{\mathcal{R}}$ in $B$
nodes.statement: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A, B\pm I, q, xI\right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(I, A^{-1}(B \pm I), q, Ax\right)$.
conclusions: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A, B\pm I, q, xI\right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(I, A^{-1}(B \pm I), q, Ax\right)$.

nodes.name: Contiguous relation of $\overline{\mathcal{R}}$ in $A$ and $B$
nodes.statement: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A\pm I,, B\pm I, q, xI \right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}} \left(I, (A \pm I)^{-1}(B \pm I), q, (A \pm I)x\right)$.
conclusions: $\overline{\mathcal{R}}\left(A\pm I,, B\pm I, q, xI \right) = \overline{\mathcal{R}} \left(I, (A \pm I)^{-1}(B \pm I), q, (A \pm I)x\right)$.

nodes.name: Independence of $\mathcal{R}$ from hypergeometric functions
nodes.statement: The novel function $\mathcal{R}(a,b,q,x)= 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(a+bq^j\right)$ is independent from hypergeometric functions because it is obtained as a solution of DDE where as hypergeometric functions are obtained from ODEs.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{R}$ is claimed independent of hypergeometric functions since it solves a DDE, not an ODE.
